paragraphs.text: Welcome back to Tis the Podcast. I'm Thom. I'm Julia. I'm Anthony. And this is our fifth episode. This week we'll be covering Die Hard. I do have to point out that this is a week of several firsts for us, guys. This is our first Christmas movie with violence, with blood, with death, with vulgarity, with guns, with terrorists, with nudity. I mean, we're crossing a lot of firsts off of our list right here at this one. But before we get going too far, Anthony, do you want to give us a plot synopsis for those who either haven't seen the film or maybe it's been a little while? Absolutely. John McClane, a detective with the New York City Police Department, arrives in Los Angeles to attempt a Christmas reunion and reconciliation with his estranged wife, Holly, who is attending a party thrown by her employer, the Nakatomi Corporation.

After a less than ideal start to their reconciliation, a group of bank robbers led by Hans Gruber take control of the building and hold everyone hostage with the exception of John. While they plan to perform a lucrative heist, unable to escape, and with no immediate police response, John is forced to take matters into his own hands. Can John defeat the bad guys and ride off into the sunset with the love of his life? Yeah, I think that about sums up the movie. So let's start out with our histories, guys. What's your history with this movie, Anthony? I don't have a storied history with this one like I did some of the other films on our list so far. I remember seeing it at some point when I was younger and loving it immediately.

It was probably my first rated R Christmas movie I've seen. I'm pretty sure I saw it in middle school for the first time with my dad. I remember really enjoying it after the first time I saw it, and I still really enjoy it. And I make sure to watch it every year, but that's about it. What about you guys? Well, it came out in 1988, I think. So I was six when it came out. So needless to say, I did not see it until the mid-90s, just because my parents are, you know, they're good parents. I obviously didn't see it in the theater. I'm sure the first time I saw it was edited on television for many reasons. But I can share with Anthony that it was my dad that I watched it with because my mom's not so into action movies.

So I'm sure it was my dad and my brother. And I just remember unfettered access to the edited version on TV anytime it was on. So if it was on, we were watching it. And that's how it is today, right? If I'm flipping through and it's on television, I got to watch it because it's such a great movie. And it's totally timeless for me, even though there's massive amounts of shoulder pads and feathered hair. It is timeless. I love this movie. It's so much fun to watch, even with the gore and the violence. And not so much the bad words because I usually watch the edited one. But anyway, that's mine. What about you, Thom? I saw this movie first way back when I was a young 34-year-old man with my wife two Christmases ago.

We were talking and realized neither of us had ever seen this movie. And I thought, as those of you who are listening to this podcast and have not seen this movie, how in the heck is Die Hard a Christmas movie? I think, actually, I say we watched it at Christmas time. We watched it well in advance of Christmas time because we were looking for a non-Christmas Christmas movie to watch. And it was fun. We, you know, I have fond memories. My wife has her own business. So things get crazy from time to time. And this was just one of those times where we were able to just unplug, hang out and spend good quality time together. And we both loved this movie. I mean, I watched it nearly 30 years after it aired or after it premiered. And it was still good. It was still funny and oddly heartwarming and very rah-rah. Let's go America.

Yeah. So, I mean, it put in all of those weird feels along with the Christmas feels, in a way that I don't know many other movies have done. I know when I was a kid, my grandparents rented the movie, but again, being decent human beings, they did not let me watch it. So I remember wanting to see this one and Lethal Weapon, both, as a kid. We've got to add that to our list at some point. I still haven't seen it.
You still haven't seen Lethal Weapon?
Nope.
Oh, that's my favorite Mel Gibson. Lethal Weapon Mel Gibson is my favorite.
Now we definitely have to schedule it sooner rather than later.

It's now on my hold list until we get ready to film it. I want to actually have a movie that I've never seen that we can talk about, so I'll be coming at it with fresh eyes. I've seen Die Hard so many times already since I watched it a couple of years ago. It never gets old. I watched it twice last week, as a matter of fact.
So let's discuss the plot. What do you guys think?
I mean, it's a pretty typical '80s action movie.

You've got this lone renegade cop and these bad guys trying to do something heinous, and he swings in to save the day. I like that it was a very self-aware '80s action movie, because Hans Gruber refers to it multiple times throughout the movie: "What, you think you're just another American hero, like Arnold Schwarzenegger or John Wayne?" or whoever else he referenced, like the American cowboy. So the fact that it was very self-aware makes it a little less cheesy than it could have become as it aged. But like you said, it's a very typical '80s action plot, and I love it despite that.
I agree. Bruce Willis and Alan Rickman knew what they were making. It was obvious. And if I'm not mistaken, this was the film that brought both of them to light in America, correct?
This is Bruce Willis's first big role, and it was Alan Rickman's first movie role ever. He was only known for stage productions before this. So we got two film legends out of this movie.
And can I just point out, what is it now, five for five, in which a Harry Potter actor has shown up on our podcast in a Christmas role?
I was actually waiting to say that. We have not had an episode where Harry Potter has not come up yet.
And we're not complaining.
No, we are not.

I love out-of-place stories, when you have a character that's just totally out of place in some location where they're completely uncomfortable. And John McClane in Los Angeles is it. The minute he gets off the airplane, he's like, "What?" Because you've got your no-nonsense New York cop in the land of nonsense, Los Angeles. So right from the beginning, I love Bruce Willis. I guess I've loved him since this movie, because I can't think of anything I was really attached to before this one.

Right. I didn't watch Moonlighting, whatever the show was that he had on television while this movie was filming. I never watched that. I think it was kind of a rom-com, right? So this is the start of Bruce Willis for me. But him as a New Yorker is sublime, and him as a New Yorker in Los Angeles is even better.
He hammed up the accent a little bit.
Did he?

Just a little. When I put it in the other day to watch, and it must have been almost a year since I'd watched it, the first time he spoke, I was like, wow, he really hams it up. Maybe it was for the whole fish-out-of-water thing, but it took a little getting used to.

So as far as our history goes, just real quick: as Julia said, this is from 1988, so it's the late '80s. The '80s action hero has definitely been established. It's based on Roderick Thorp's novel, which had been a New York Times bestseller, and it was directed by John McTiernan. You guys know him? He did Predator, The Hunt for Red October, The 13th Warrior, and The Thomas Crown Affair, which has haunted me my entire life, because I can't tell you how many people spell Thom Crowe as Thomas Crown because of that film. And he directed an awful 2002 film, Rollerball, starring LL Cool J. Did you guys see that one? It's just terrible. Ladies may love Cool James, but I'm not sure they did in that movie. It was bad.
Red October was really good. I like that movie. I mean, he has a good resume besides that. What was it, Rollerball? But the rest of those films you've rattled off are all pretty good.

For sure. Let's just jump right into the cast, guys. I think we're going to spend a lot more time here than we have in the past on other episodes, because we have an amazing cast, starting with, of course, Bruce Willis. So this was your first experience with Bruce Willis, Julia?
Die Hard was, yeah, that I can remember.

Just given my age and the types of movies he was in, yeah, this was my start with Bruce Willis. But once I started, I didn't stop. I love Bruce Willis all the way through the rest of this film series, right? Which got worse later, except for the first three. So you've got the first Die Hard, the second Die Hard, the third Die Hard. I love number one, and then I love number three, and then I love number two, in that order. And I love three so much because of Samuel L. Jackson, because I love Samuel L. Jackson.
Oh, Bruce Willis and Samuel L. Jackson do so well together.
It's just so fantastic. But I don't like the newer ones nearly as much. I still watch them.

I'm going to repeat the argument that Michael Scott made on The Office, talking about Die Hard. The first few were really good because he was just an ordinary guy forced into these extraordinary circumstances. But as each movie went on, he became more and more like a freaking superhero, with the things they were having him do. It was much better when he was just a cop stuck at a Christmas party who had to save the day.
There's always a way to bring it back to Michael Scott.
I have to do it.
Especially since you're still watching it.

That's right. There's a new Die Hard coming out, Die Hard: Year One, and Bruce Willis is rumored to be in it. Nothing's confirmed yet. I couldn't find much about it except for the fact that it's been announced.
It sounds like a prequel. Year One.
It does. So I guess he would have to be playing somebody else. I'm not sure who he would be playing in the film.
I'm so confused by that title. Maybe it's about his days as a cop in New York.
I don't know. His first Christmas where he had to stop terrorists.
Yeah, that's what I immediately think of.
So is this your favorite Bruce Willis film, guys?

This is my favorite. I'm going to have to deviate here. It's yours. I am. I really loved Unbreakable. I mean. Oh, good choice. And I was a big fan of 12 Monkeys. I thought it was a great film. I loved it. I have not seen it in years, so I don't know if I still do, but I was a big fan. As an Unbreakable fan, what did you think of the ending of Split? Haven't seen it. Oh, okay. Never mind. But, you know. It's a very good movie. You should go watch it. I'll watch any M. Night movie for the most part, you know. I've lost faith in the man. Have you? After I saw the last one with the grandparents, I'm done. Oh, I liked that one. I thought that one was okay. Which one? Did I miss one entirely? It came out like last summer. The Visit.
I remember the trailers for that. I didn't know Split was an M. Night Shyamalan movie.
Oh, yeah. It is.
Okay. All right. So that's his most recent one, then. Sorry, I know we deviated there.
But I would also feel remiss if we didn't bring up that he was in Look Who's Talking, and Beavis and Butt-Head Do America. Was that their movie?
I did not like that show or that movie.
You didn't like Beavis and Butt-Head?
No, I did not.
I never watched it, but I can quote it.
And he was also in Armageddon, which was kind of a big deal when we were younger. I liked Armageddon.
Yeah, that's right. I forgot about that. But one of the things I really loved is all of the short-term characters he's done on TV.
Like Friends. He was great on that show.

Yes, he was. And in researching for the show, I also learned he was the first fill-in host for David Letterman, back in 2003, when David Letterman, for the first time in 20 years, had a sick day. Bruce Willis was supposed to be the guest, and they talked to him, and he filled in for Letterman. And we do have somebody to thank for Bruce Willis's casting in this movie, and it's not the director.
Who is that?
It's somebody I never thought I would thank in my life: Rupert Murdoch.
What?
Bruce Willis wouldn't do it below a certain salary, and as head of Fox, Rupert Murdoch personally approved the salary and the budget for the film.
Was this the one where he made $5 million?

Yeah, something like that. I forget the exact amount, but Rupert Murdoch personally approved it, allowing Bruce Willis to star in the film. So thanks, Rupert Murdoch. It's the only good thing you've ever done.
Oh, burn.
If you're listening, by the way, you can come on our show and be a guest host if you'd like. Please come on our show. I have a few things I want to talk about with you.
Are they related to Christmas movies?
I can tie them back. I can tie it back to Home Alone 2.
Okay, okay.
And we should also mention, Bruce Willis was not the first choice for this part. Do you know who was, Julia?
I don't know who the first choice was, so tell me.
Robert De Niro.
Okay, so I was right. That would be a crazy different movie.
Another Christmas film in which Robert De Niro was offered the role first and turned it down. Schwarzenegger was also approached for it.
That makes sense. I didn't know that, though. It makes it even funnier that Alan Rickman brought up Arnold Schwarzenegger.
And did you guys recognize his wife from anything else?
She looked familiar, but I can't name anything else she's been in off the top of my head. She's definitely one of those people I know I've seen in something else.
You've seen her really recently, in a TV show. One that Julia liked more than I did?
I was blown away too, guys, I'm not going to lie. She played Camille Braverman on Parenthood.
Oh, I haven't watched Parenthood. I've never watched the show.
Never mind, then. Oh, I thought we talked about it. It must have been somebody else. My bad.
I'm sure I would like it.
Are we so interchangeable with other people, Thom? I thought the three of us had a special connection as co-hosts, and you're getting us confused with other people.
We do, but as Julia will vouch, when you have a child, you lose sleep, and everything in life becomes a fog and one big constant memory.
Holly is played by Bonnie Bedelia. Do you know who she's related to from a Christmas movie we talked about recently? Is she related to Catherine O'Hara?
That was just my first guess, but I have no clue. She is Macaulay Culkin's aunt.
Is she really?
She is.
How funny. I didn't know that.
She doesn't have as illustrious a career as Bruce Willis, but she is in an upcoming Christmas movie called Christmas on the Coast that's currently filming.
Is that a theatrical release or a Hallmark release?
You know, I am honestly not sure. Judging from the name, it sounds like something that would be a made-for-television movie.
Yeah, it sounds a bit Hallmark-y.
It does sound Hallmark-y, doesn't it? Which is not a bad thing, by the way.

So, Holly. I think she is an amazing character, and she has one of the best scenes in this movie, and that is when she confronts Hans Gruber for the first time. She can just hold her own against him and negotiate with him, and he has the utmost respect for her and just about tells her so to her face. I love that scene. She held her own against him better than John McClane did in any other scene in this film.

That is a great scene. She has one of the best lines there, too. Do you guys remember the line? If you don't like things messy, you might want to start bringing us to the bathroom. I know that wasn't the one, but I always love that one because I'm like, straight up what a woman would say.
I love when she's prepping for it and she's talking about it. She's like, "Hey, babe, I negotiate million-dollar deals for breakfast. I think I can handle this Eurotrash."
Anyone else love the irony that her name's Holly and it's a Christmas movie? Because I'm fighting to the death that it's a Christmas movie.

No, we haven't gotten to that yet. But yeah, I love her. Her character is super awesome. What cracked me up, though, about rewatching this movie again is that office culture in the '80s cracks me up a little bit. Because who is at a Christmas party on Christmas Eve at your office, for one? I mean, don't they schedule that early now, so that on Christmas Eve you're actually with your kids? Is there a difference between the '80s generation and Gen Xers now, where we're like…
Scott Calvin was also at a Christmas party on Christmas Eve.
It was Christmas Eve, wasn't it? It was.
So listeners, if you're out there and your office throws Christmas parties like Christmas Eve, please write in and tell us how terrible the company you work for is.

I also think it's so funny, and kind of sad, that she was talking to her kids on the phone on Christmas Eve from the party, and she's like, "Well, I'm probably not going to see you guys before you go to bed, so I love you." And I'm like, it's Christmas Eve, and you're not going to see your kids before they go to bed? This is what working women in the '80s had to do. They had to get it done.
Which women still have to do.
Yeah, they do.

It does bring up a good point: why in the heck hasn't John seen his kids? He goes to this party instead of going to see them on Christmas Eve. That's just weird. As a dad, I am not going to see my estranged wife at her Christmas party before I see my kids.
But the whole point was he wanted to work things out with his wife. So I'm going to argue he did that in the hopes he could go home with her and surprise the kids that way.
That's valid. I could see that.
So Santa's bringing Daddy home.
That's one way to put it.
I think we should hold off. Before we get to our favorite actor for this film, I just have to throw a little bit of love out there to Reginald VelJohnson.

Now, Reginald VelJohnson is no stranger to Christmas movies, guys. Really? He has been in a movie called A Cool Like That Christmas, The Twelve Dog Days Till Christmas, The Mistletones, and they're currently prepping the movie The Flight Before Christmas. So he's got a little bit of a Christmas movie interest there. I did love his character, but did you know one of the only bad reviews for this film came from Roger Ebert, who said he loved the entire movie, but this specific character and actor ruined it for him and took him out of the movie every time he was on the screen. So he gave it like one or two star rating because of this one character, even though he loved the rest of the film. There's a reason I don't listen to film critics, and I think you just spouted one of the good ones.

Seriously. He gave this movie a horrible rating because of Reginald VelJohnson? That's correct. Which is weird because I think he added, in my mind, he is essential to the plot of this movie. He is John's guy on the outside. He's the guy John is connecting with. They have a really sweet moment about midway, three quarters of the way through the film, where he's, John McClane's like giving up and he's on the walkie telling him, look, this is what you've got to tell my wife. You'll know what I mean in a bit. You'll know who she is in a bit. And it's a really sweet scene. And he's basically trying to put the fight back in John. I love that scene. And I love the character and he's awesome. And utmost respect to Roger Ebert, but he was totally off the mark this time.

Okay, wait a second. Roger Ebert didn't like Dwayne Robinson. He didn't like Chief Dwayne Robinson, not Reginald. Because when I first read that trivia bit, I thought the same thing that you just said. And I was like, man, what is up with this? Because I'm not, I mean, I was the same things, right? Like, how could you not like that guy? He didn't like Robinson. And Robinson was like the biggest dirtbag character in this entire movie. So I can see his points on that because he really is kind of pointless. And he's totally inept for a chief of any, I mean, like nothing he says makes sense. He's just there for you to not like him. He made me very angry just to look at him. Just like that newscaster.
But he was another 80s movie stereotype. Just like the jerky office worker, or what was his name? Ellis.
Very true. Very, yeah. Total stereotypes. That hard beat chief that you have to deal with?

That was pretty 80s. But I apologize for getting that wrong. So thanks for correcting me, Julia. But I still am going to say that Roger Ebert missed the mark here. I mean, to take the movie down that much because you don't like the police chief.

I can't even really see dinging the movie over his character. He wasn't that big of a presence in the movie to even lower a rating for. If you're going to ding it, no more than half a star, honestly. If that.
Yeah. So, should we go on to our favorite?
Let's do it. Please. Hans Gruber. Alan Rickman.
Oh. Not the first choice for his role either.
No. Did you know he also wasn't the first choice for Snape?
I didn't know that.
The studio wanted Tim Roth.
I like Tim Roth, but I couldn't see him as Snape.
I was going to say, dodged a bullet, because Lie to Me is one of my favorite shows ever, and that would not have happened with Tim Roth had he been Snape. So it worked out well for everybody.
So who was first picked for Hans Gruber?
Sam Neill, a.k.a. Dr. Alan Grant from Jurassic Park. Oh, that's right.

I can see him in a similar role, but it would have been a very different portrayal of the villain. Rickman was firing on all cylinders in this film. They had to convince Rickman to take the role, though, because he was afraid, and rightfully so, as it turned out, given his future movie roles, that if he played a big Hollywood bad villain, he'd be typecast as such. And sure enough, he was in many of his roles later on in life.
But totally worth it because nobody plays a bad villain like Alan Rickman does. No, not at all. But with depth too.

I love it. He does. Even when he did, when he was the Sheriff of Nottingham in Robin Hood, Prince of Thieves, I loved it. He wasn't going to do that one either. Did you know that? He wasn't? He wasn't going to do that until they told him, carte blanche, this is your character, you make it happen. Oh, that makes me like even more. That character is all Alan Rickman's creation. Why a spoon, cousin? Because it'll hurt more, you twit. Whatever he calls him. We quote that all the time in the office. Why a spoon, cousin? Nobody has ever made ho, ho, ho sound more intimidating than Alan Rickman. when he said it in that voice. Ho, ho, ho, ho. I love it. Aside from that, Snape, I don't even know where to start with this guy's film pedigree.

I mean, he's done amazing stuff. He was one of the first famous people that, when they died and I heard about it, I started crying. It hit me bad that day. I didn't know the guy personally. I've just seen him through his work and through his quotes about the stuff he's worked on. But he seemed like he would have been just as cool in person as he was on the screen.
And so much of that is Snape, right? That's my biggest attachment to Alan Rickman. I got super emotional when I found out that he had died. Just terribly sad. What a loss.

And not to get on a Harry Potter Snape thing, but we always have to get on a Harry Potter thing on this podcast. Reading the books, he's not who I would have pictured as Snape before he was cast, because in the book, Snape is, I think, younger and has more of a fiery, easily angered personality, whereas Alan Rickman brought this menacing calm to the character. So it was a different portrayal than I would have imagined or cast for that character.

But now reading those books, all I can picture is Alan Rickman as Snape. When those movies are eventually remade in like 30 years, nobody will be able to top his performance. I can totally agree. Just like if this movie's ever remained, nobody's ever going to be able to top his performance here either.
I have a fairly unpopular opinion about not being able to top people in movies, especially the Harry Potter ones. I don't think Michael Gambon ever lived up to Richard Harris.
100% agree.
Awesome. I have had people argue that hardcore. Still, when I read the book, I'm picturing Richard Harris every step of the way as Dumbledore.

Sarah argues that she likes Richard Harris better in the role and thinks he is Dumbledore, but she thinks Michael Gambon brought something Harris didn't have, in terms of his youthful eccentricities. Richard Harris is very regal and old, whereas Michael Gambon brought that different aspect of Dumbledore from the books, which is his kookier side.

So she thought like if you could combine the two, like Richard Harris's looks and demeanor, but with Gambon's quirks, like it would have been like the perfect combination. It would have been interesting to see what Richard Harris would have made of the line where they talk about Bertie Botts beans and Dumbledore. I wonder what he would have sounded like reading that line because you're true. It's very true, right? That playfulness. It's not, there's not much of that in the first one, just because there's not because it's the first one. I would have been very interested to see how he would have done in the later movies where he gets a little more jovial. I wonder if part of that was the detached newness of Harry with Dumbledore.

Yeah, that's true. We're going to have to stop talking about Harry Potter or we're going to have nothing to talk about when we get to those Christmas scenes. Oh, my God. Can we just make that like a three-hour episode? Because we have a lot to say. Maybe we should make it its own standalone, not part of anything else. have like a 6.5 episode just through Harry Potter so we can get it on the books.
Alan Rickman's other Christmas movie we'll be covering in February: Love Actually.
Love that movie. He and Emma Thompson just had great, great chemistry, even though, as a couple, they were not supposed to have great chemistry. Just as actors, they did such a great job.
And it's just weird thinking that Snape and Trelawney were lovers in another movie.
Oh, it is.
Or that Trelawney and, gosh, what's his name, Kenneth Branagh's character, Gilderoy Lockhart…
Yeah, that they were lovers in a different movie.
Right. In Much Ado About Nothing, he was Benedick and she was Beatrice.
Yep. They have a long history, though, as well.
I think it's that whole six degrees of separation… Kevin Costner? No, not Kevin Costner. Kevin Bacon. That Kevin Bacon thing.
I think it's like two degrees of separation for Harry Potter, guys, as we're learning. Or any Brits, for that matter.
That should totally be a page on our website. Two Degrees of Separation from Harry Potter. And we point out how each movie is connected.
That could be fun. That could be a lot of fun. I like it.

Anyway. Hans Gruber. Alan Rickman. What blew me away about his performance… I mean, he was great throughout the entire thing, but the scene where he confronts John on the roof, and he's pretending to be an escaped hostage, when he pulls off speaking like an American, he nails it perfectly. Not everybody can do that as well as he did. I mean, the German comes and goes throughout the film, let's be honest. It's not the most consistent accent. But when he switches to an American dialect, I was shocked. I didn't know Alan Rickman had that in him. That's one of my favorite scenes in the movie.

I read some trivia that it had a lot to do with him being cast as well. The director, McTiernan, heard that American accent, I don't remember how, in the process of auditioning, and that clinched it for him, because they had to figure out a way for John McClane and Hans Gruber to meet in the movie. At what point do they meet? How are they going to manufacture that? And that became the way to do it. His ability to sound so American made that happen, which I think is also pretty cool.

So the scene where he falls from the building: awesome scene. But did you know that's a real look of surprise on his face? The stuntmen were supposed to drop him on the count of three or something, and they dropped him early to get the surprise. And supposedly, Alan Rickman was none too pleased about it when he hit the ground.
Yeah. He fell 20 feet, right?
Yeah, it was a good height. Twenty feet onto an air pad.
Yeah. He was not happy about being tricked to get that.
That's a bold move on the director's part, or the stuntman, whoever made that decision. The stunt director. That's a bold move to make.

Well, if that was his first movie… Could you imagine if somebody did that to him toward the end of his career, like as Snape, or in his later movies? If somebody pulled that with him, he probably could get somebody fired.
I would think there would be somebody who would never work in Hollywood again.
But can we talk about the logistics of that scene? Because I don't really buy that he was hanging on by a watch.
Yeah, that always makes me laugh.
It's a really good watch, guys. It's not this cheap Apple Watch 3 that was just announced. He never could have held on by that.
It's one of those gun-on-the-mantelpiece moments as well. There are a few in this movie, but that watch is one of them. At the beginning, they mention her getting a Rolex.
A Rolex, right. Wasn't that the Rolex?
Yep.
Right, exactly.

Who was the other one? Oh, Reginald talking about, I haven't shot a gun since, right? His whole mishap and all that. The minute he says that, I think even the first time I saw it, I was like, he's going to shoot a gun. He's going to kill someone. It's going to happen.
It's a plot device right there. He's going to shoot them.

Yeah, there were a few. I mean, this movie is really not without its flaws and its mistakes. Do we want to move on to what we liked and didn't like in the film? Wait, can we talk about one more character?
Argyle.
I was looking at Argyle, the limo driver. I love Argyle. He's so great. It just breaks down my jaw.

When he rams the van at the end, when he gets to play the hero and he jumps out of the limo and just decks the guy. I love it. I feel like the ending is made completely by him. They get in the limo and drive away, and there's that whole smashed-up front of the car, and he just goes, like nothing's wrong.
Right. His quote right at the very end: "If this is your idea of Christmas, I gotta be here for New Year's."

Yeah. He was great from the get-go, when he's telling Bruce Willis that he's never done this before, picked somebody up and driven the limo, and Bruce Willis is like, "Yeah, I've never ridden in a limo before." They just immediately start out on a good note.
And he has excellent taste in Christmas music, might I add. "Christmas in Hollis."
"Christmas in Hollis." I started cracking up when I heard that and thought of you, Anthony.

Yeah, I'm glad. And then I thought of you guys, because I feel like you guys kind of judged me for that choice. And Bruce Willis says to him, "Don't you have any Christmas music?" And he says, "This is Christmas music." So I did think of you guys too.
